title: What Makes a One-hit Wonder?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss the one-hit wonder phenomenon, based on a HowStuffWorks article by Chuck. They trace the phrase's print origin (1970 usage about ABBA, though it may have been used earlier), the generally held definition (a single Billboard Top 40 hit), and how the definition blurs: artists with one hit who are still considered legendary, one-hit wonders who were hits only in other countries, and songs that were cultural hits without chart success. They walk through one-hit wonders decade by decade from the 1950s through the 1990s, then cover sports (Chris Jelic, Eddie Gaedel), art (Harvey Ball's smiley face, Grant Wood's American Gothic), and books and film (Harper Lee, J.D. Salinger, John Kennedy Toole, Sylvia Plath, Joseph Heller, Michael Cimino, Steve Gordon). The episode closes with a listener mail from Devon, whose wife Elizabeth thinks the show is stoner banter, and a sign-off with social and contact info.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the one-hit wonder topic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, joke about Chuck's name and on-air freeze-up, and introduce the one-hit wonder topic from Chuck's article. Josh notes there is little scholarly work on the subject and mentions a fan site listing one-hit wonders by year.

segments.title: Origin of the phrase and the Billboard Top 40 definition
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the phrase's origin: a 1970 print use about ABBA cited by phrases.org, which says it was likely already in use. They cover the generally held definition, which requires a Billboard Top 40 hit, and note how the definition gets blurry.

segments.title: Legendary artists who only had one hit
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck list well-known artists with only one chart hit, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Garth Brooks as Chris Gaines, Beck, the White Stripes, Lou Reed, and Iggy Pop. They note that some one-hit wonders had no Top 40 hit but still defined a moment, such as Wall of Voodoo's Mexican Radio, Modern English, and the Weather Girls.

segments.title: One-hit wonders by decade, 1950s to 1990s
segments.summary: The hosts run through one-hit wonders across the decades: the Penguins' Earth Angel in the fifties, Blue Cheer and the Lemon Pipers in the sixties, Norman Greenbaum and Brewer and Shipley in the seventies, Soft Cell, Tony Basil and Bow Wow Wow in the eighties, and Crash Test Dummies, the Macarena, and Faith No More in the nineties. They also discuss disco-era one-hit wonders and bands like Lips Inc. and Pseudo Echo with the same song, Funky Town.

segments.title: Hits abroad: one-hit wonders in the US versus Europe
segments.summary: The hosts discuss bands that were big outside the US but considered one-hit wonders in America, including Aha, Right Said Fred, Frankie Goes to Hollywood, Gary Numan, and Falco. They note that the term can feel dismissive to artists with long careers abroad.

segments.title: One-hit wonders in sports and art
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sports one-hit wonders, including players with a single home run and Eddie Gaedel, a little person who drew four walks for the Yankees in 1951. They also cover art one-hit wonders: Harvey Ball, creator of the smiley face for a 1971 campaign for the State Mutual Life Assurance company, and Grant Wood, who painted American Gothic.

segments.title: One-hit wonders in literature and film
segments.summary: The hosts discuss authors with one famous book, including Harper Lee (To Kill a Mockingbird), J.D. Salinger, Sylvia Plath, Joseph Heller, and John Kennedy Toole (A Confederacy of Dunces). They also cover filmmakers Michael Cimino (The Deer Hunter, Heaven's Gate) and Steve Gordon (Arthur), and Chuck and Josh's views on the Arthur remake.

segments.title: Listener mail from Devon about Elizabeth
segments.summary: Devon writes that his wife Elizabeth thinks the show is stoner banter and prefers This American Life and Radio Lab. He asks for a shout-out to her. Josh and Chuck push back on the stoner claim and agree to consider the request.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give ways to get in touch: Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
